reminder: A Shimura variety is an arithmetic quotient of a Hermitian symmetric domain, as a [modular curve](c:modular-curve) is a quotient of the upper half plane.
definition: A Shimura datum $(G,X)$ consists of a [reductive group](c:reductive-group) $G$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ and a $G(\mathbb{R})$-conjugacy class $X$ of homomorphisms $\mathbb{S}\to G_{\mathbb{R}}$ from the Deligne torus that obey Deligne's axioms; then $X$ is a finite union of [Hermitian symmetric spaces](c:hermitian-symmetric-space). For a small compact open subgroup $K\subset G(\mathbb{A}_f)$, where $\mathbb{A}_f$ is the ring of finite [adeles](c:adele), the Shimura variety is $\mathrm{Sh}_K(G,X)=G(\mathbb{Q})\backslash(X\times G(\mathbb{A}_f)/K)$. Its complex points form a finite disjoint union of quotients $\Gamma\backslash X^+$ by [arithmetic groups](c:arithmetic-group) $\Gamma$, and it is an [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) over a number field.
examples: Take $G=\mathrm{GL}_2$ and $X=\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}$, which is two copies of the upper half plane: the Shimura varieties are the [modular curves](c:modular-curve) of level $K$.

Take $G=\mathrm{GSp}_{2g}$: the Shimura varieties are the Siegel modular varieties, which parametrize principally polarized [abelian varieties](c:abelian-variety) of dimension $g$ with level structure.
Non-example: the quotient of hyperbolic $3$-space by an arithmetic group (a Bianchi orbifold) is not a Shimura variety, because hyperbolic $3$-space is not Hermitian and has no complex structure.

steps: Take the Shimura datum with $G=\mathrm{GL}_2$ and $X$ the union of the upper and lower half planes.
Choose a compact open subgroup $K$ of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f)$ as the level.
The quotient $\mathrm{Sh}_K$ is a finite union of curves $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}$ with $\Gamma$ a [congruence subgroup](c:congruence-subgroup).
So each modular curve is a one-dimensional Shimura variety.
links.why: It shows that Shimura varieties extend the theory of modular curves to other groups and higher dimension.

reminder: A space is sigma-compact when it is a countable union of [compact](c:compact-space) subspaces.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is sigma-compact when $X=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}K_n$ for a [countable](c:countable-set) family of [compact](c:compact-space) subspaces $K_n$. One can then take the sequence increasing, $K_1\subseteq K_2\subseteq\cdots$, by replacing $K_n$ with $K_1\cup\dots\cup K_n$.
examples: Every compact space is sigma-compact, and so is $\mathbb{R}^n$, which is the union of the closed balls of radius $k$ for $k=1,2,\dots$.
The rationals $\mathbb{Q}$ are sigma-compact, because $\mathbb{Q}$ is a countable union of single points.
Non-example: an uncountable discrete space is not sigma-compact, because its compact subsets are finite and countably many finite sets cover only a countable set.

steps: Let $X$ be a compact space.
Put $K_n=X$ for every $n$.
Then $X$ is the union of the sequence $(K_n)$ of compact subspaces.
So every compact space is sigma-compact, and sigma-compactness allows countably many pieces.
links.why: It shows that sigma-compactness weakens compactness to countably many compact pieces.

steps: Let $X=\bigcup_nK_n$ with each $K_n$ compact, and let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open cover of $X$.
By compactness, a finite subfamily $\mathcal{U}_n$ of $\mathcal{U}$ covers each $K_n$.
The union of the countably many finite families $\mathcal{U}_n$ is countable and still covers $X$.
So every open cover of $X$ has a countable subcover, and $X$ is Lindelöf.
links.why: It shows that every theorem about Lindelöf spaces applies to sigma-compact spaces.

reminder: A family of subsets is sigma-locally finite when it is a countable union of locally finite families.
definition: A family $\mathcal{B}$ of subsets of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is sigma-locally finite when $\mathcal{B}=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{B}_n$ and each $\mathcal{B}_n$ is a [locally finite family](c:locally-finite-family). A family is locally finite when every point of $X$ has a neighbourhood that meets only finitely many members of it.
examples: Every locally finite family is sigma-locally finite: take all $\mathcal{B}_n$ equal to it.
Every countable family of subsets is sigma-locally finite, because a family with one member is locally finite.
A [metrizable space](c:metrizable-space) has a sigma-locally finite [base](c:topological-base), and a regular Hausdorff space with such a base is metrizable (the Nagata-Smirnov theorem).

Non-example: the family of all one-point subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ is not sigma-locally finite, because a locally finite subfamily has only finitely many points in each bounded interval, so it is countable, and countably many countable sets cannot cover $\mathbb{R}$.

steps: Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a locally finite family of subsets of $X$.
Put $\mathcal{B}_n=\mathcal{B}$ for every $n$.
Then $\mathcal{B}$ is a countable union of locally finite families.
So a locally finite family is the special case with one piece.
links.why: It shows that sigma-local finiteness weakens local finiteness to countably many pieces.

reminder: The signature of a permutation is $+1$ if it is a product of an even number of transpositions and $-1$ if the number is odd.
definition: Every [permutation](c:permutation) $\sigma$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is a product of [transpositions](c:transposition), and the parity of the number $k$ of factors depends only on $\sigma$. The signature is $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)=(-1)^k$; it is the unique [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) from the [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group) $S_n$ to $\{+1,-1\}$ that sends every transposition to $-1$.
examples: A transposition has signature $-1$.
A $3$-cycle is a product of two transpositions, $(1\,2\,3)=(1\,3)(1\,2)$, so its signature is $+1$.
The [permutation matrix](c:permutation-matrix) of $\sigma$ has [determinant](c:determinant) $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$.
Non-example: the map that sends every permutation to $+1$ is a homomorphism but not the signature, because it sends transpositions to $+1$.

steps: Take the symmetric group $S_n$ and the group $\{+1,-1\}$ under multiplication.
Define $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)=(-1)^k$ when $\sigma$ is a product of $k$ transpositions.
Joining a product of $k$ transpositions to one of $l$ transpositions gives a product of $k+l$ transpositions.
So $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma\tau)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)$, and sgn is a homomorphism.
links.why: It shows that the signature is a homomorphism, so the sign of a product is the product of the signs.

steps: Send $\sigma$ to its [permutation matrix](c:permutation-matrix) $P_\sigma$, which permutes the standard basis vectors.
Swapping two basis vectors swaps two columns, so $\det P_\tau=-1$ for a transposition $\tau$.
The determinant is multiplicative, and every $\sigma$ is a product of transpositions.
So $\det P_\sigma=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$, and the signature is the determinant on permutation matrices.
links.why: It shows where the signs in the Leibniz formula for the determinant come from.

reminder: A simplicial presheaf on a site is a contravariant functor from the site to simplicial sets.
definition: A simplicial presheaf on a [site](c:grothendieck-site) $S$ is a [presheaf](c:presheaf) of [simplicial sets](c:simplicial-set), that is, a [functor](c:functor) $F:S^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{sSet}$. Equivalently, it is a family of presheaves of sets $F_n$ on $S$ with face and degeneracy maps that are natural in $S$.
examples: Every presheaf of sets is a simplicial presheaf when you regard each set $F(U)$ as a discrete simplicial set.
For a simplicial set $K$, the constant simplicial presheaf sends every object $U$ of $S$ to $K$.
For an open cover $\{U_i\}$ of a space $X$, the Čech nerve is a simplicial presheaf on the open sets of $X$.
Non-example: a covariant functor $S\to\mathrm{sSet}$ is not a simplicial presheaf, because the maps must run backwards along the morphisms of $S$.

steps: Start with a [presheaf](c:presheaf) $F$ of sets on $S$.
View each set $F(U)$ as a discrete simplicial set, with only degenerate simplices above degree $0$.
A restriction map of $F$ is then a map of simplicial sets.
So $F$ is a simplicial presheaf, and the general case allows higher simplices.
links.why: It shows that ordinary presheaves are the discrete simplicial presheaves.

steps: Start with a [simplicial sheaf](c:simplicial-sheaf) $F$ on $S$.
Each $F_n$ is a sheaf, so in particular a presheaf of sets.
The face and degeneracy maps are natural transformations of presheaves.
So $F$ is a simplicial presheaf, and a simplicial sheaf adds the sheaf condition in each degree.
links.why: It shows what a simplicial sheaf adds: the gluing condition in every simplicial degree.

reminder: The $n$-skeleton of a simplicial set is the smallest simplicial subset that contains all its simplices of dimension at most $n$.
definition: For a [simplicial set](c:simplicial-set) $X$ and $n\ge0$, the skeleton $\mathrm{sk}_nX$ is the simplicial subset generated by the simplices of $X$ of dimension at most $n$. Equivalently, let $i:\Delta_{\le n}\to\Delta$ be the inclusion of the [full subcategory](c:full-subcategory) of the [simplex category](c:simplex-category) on $[0],\dots,[n]$; then $\mathrm{sk}_n=i_!i^*$, where $i^*$ is restriction and $i_!$ is left [Kan extension](c:kan-extension). The coskeleton $\mathrm{cosk}_n=i_*i^*$ uses the right Kan extension.
examples: For the standard $2$-simplex $\Delta^2$, the skeleton $\mathrm{sk}_1\Delta^2$ is the boundary $\partial\Delta^2$, whose non-degenerate simplices are the three vertices and three edges.
The skeleton $\mathrm{sk}_0X$ is the discrete simplicial set on the vertices of $X$.
A simplicial set $X$ equals $\mathrm{sk}_nX$ exactly when it has no non-degenerate simplex of dimension above $n$.
Non-example: the horn $\Lambda^2_1\subset\Delta^2$, which has only two edges, is not a skeleton of $\Delta^2$, because $\mathrm{sk}_1\Delta^2$ contains all three edges.

steps: Let $i:\Delta_{\le n}\to\Delta$ be the inclusion of the full subcategory on $[0],\dots,[n]$.
Restrict the simplicial set $X$ along $i$ to get the truncation $i^*X$.
Take the left Kan extension $i_!i^*X$ of this truncation along $i$.
The result is $\mathrm{sk}_nX$, so a skeleton is a left Kan extension of a truncation.
links.why: It shows that skeleta come from the general Kan extension machinery, with its adjunctions.

reminder: Singular cohomology of a space is the cohomology of the cochains that assign coefficients to singular simplices.
definition: For a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ and an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $A$, let $C_n(X)$ be the free abelian group on the singular $n$-simplices $\Delta^n\to X$; with the alternating sum of faces as boundary, $C_\bullet(X)$ is a [chain complex](c:chain-complex). The singular cohomology $H^n(X;A)$ is the $n$-th [cohomology](c:cohomology) of the [cochain complex](c:cochain-complex) $\mathrm{Hom}(C_\bullet(X),A)$.
examples: For a point, $H^0=A$ and $H^n=0$ for $n>0$.
For the circle, $H^n(S^1;\mathbb{Z})$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ for $n=0,1$ and $0$ for $n\ge2$.
The ring $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^\infty;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ is the polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z}/2[x]$ with $x$ in degree $1$.
Non-example: [Čech cohomology](c:cech-cohomology) uses open covers, not singular simplices; for the Warsaw circle the singular cohomology is that of a point, but the Čech group $H^1$ is $\mathbb{Z}$.

steps: Singular cohomology $H^n(-;A)$ is a contravariant functor from spaces to abelian groups.
It is homotopy invariant and exact on pairs, and it satisfies excision and additivity.
So it satisfies the axioms of a generalized cohomology theory.
It also satisfies the dimension axiom, $H^n(\mathrm{pt};A)=0$ for $n\ne0$, which the general case omits.
links.why: It shows that singular cohomology is the generalized theory fixed by the dimension axiom.

reminder: The six operations are the functors $f^*$, $f_*$, $f_!$, $f^!$, tensor product and internal hom, with adjunctions and base change between them.
definition: A six-functor formalism gives, for every space $X$, a [derived category](c:derived-category) $D(X)$ with a [tensor product](c:tensor-product) $\otimes$ and an internal hom that are adjoint. For every map $f:X\to Y$ it gives functors with $f^*\dashv f_*$ and $f_!\dashv f^!$, which are [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) pairs. These satisfy [base change](c:base-change), the projection formula $f_!(A\otimes f^*B)\cong f_!A\otimes B$, and $f_!\cong f_*$ when $f$ is proper.
examples: Étale sheaves with $\ell$-adic coefficients on schemes of finite type over a separably closed field form a six-functor formalism.
Sheaves on locally compact Hausdorff spaces, with $f_!$ the direct image with compact support, give the six operations, and $f^!$ gives Verdier duality.
Non-example: the pair $f^*\dashv f_*$ of sheaves alone has only two of the six operations, with no $f_!$, no $f^!$ and no tensor product, so it is not a six-functor formalism.

reminder: A square matrix $A$ is skew-symmetric when $A^T=-A$.
definition: A [square matrix](c:square-matrix) $A=(a_{ij})$ is skew-symmetric when its [transpose](c:transpose-matrix) is its negative, $A^T=-A$, that is, $a_{ji}=-a_{ij}$ for all $i,j$. In a ring where $2$ is not a zero divisor, all diagonal entries are then $0$.
examples: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ is skew-symmetric.
Every $3\times3$ skew-symmetric matrix has the form $\begin{pmatrix}0&a&b\\-a&0&c\\-b&-c&0\end{pmatrix}$, and such a matrix represents the cross product with a vector.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\-2&1\end{pmatrix}$ over the real numbers is not skew-symmetric, because its diagonal entries are not $0$.

steps: Start with a [square matrix](c:square-matrix) $A=(a_{ij})$.
Add the condition $a_{ji}=-a_{ij}$ for all $i$ and $j$.
Over the real numbers this forces every diagonal entry to be $0$.
Then $A$ is skew-symmetric, so its entries above the diagonal fix all its entries.
links.why: It shows that a skew-symmetric matrix is a square matrix with the transpose condition, so it has only $n(n-1)/2$ free entries.

reminder: A skyscraper sheaf at a point $x$ gives a group $A$ on open sets that contain $x$ and the trivial group elsewhere.
definition: Let $X$ be a [topological space](c:topological-space), $x\in X$ a point and $A$ an [abelian group](c:abelian-group). The skyscraper sheaf $i_{x*}A$ assigns $A$ to each [open set](c:open-set) $U$ with $x\in U$ and the trivial group to every other open set, with identity restriction maps between open sets that contain $x$. It is the [direct image](c:direct-image) of the constant [sheaf](c:sheaf) $A$ on the one-point space $\{x\}$ under the inclusion $i_x:\{x\}\to X$.
examples: On $X=\mathbb{R}$ with $x=0$ and $A=\mathbb{Z}$, the sections over $(-1,1)$ are $\mathbb{Z}$ and the sections over $(1,2)$ are $0$.
On a Riemann surface, the skyscraper sheaf $\mathbb{C}_p$ at a point $p$ is the quotient of the sheaf of holomorphic functions by the subsheaf of functions that vanish at $p$.
Non-example: in $\mathbb{R}$, the direct sum of the skyscraper sheaves at two different points $x$ and $y$ has support on two points, so it is not a skyscraper sheaf at one point.

steps: Define $F(U)=A$ if $x\in U$ and $F(U)=0$ otherwise, with identity restriction maps between sets that contain $x$.
Let $\{U_i\}$ cover $U$ and let $(s_i)$ be sections that agree on overlaps.
The $s_i$ with $x\in U_i$ are equal elements of $A$, and the other $s_i$ are $0$.
So the family glues uniquely, and $F$ is a sheaf with support the closure of $\{x\}$.
links.why: It shows that the skyscraper sheaf is a sheaf, and a simple one to compute with.

reminder: An $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ representation is a vector space with operators $E$, $F$ and $H$ that obey the bracket relations of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$.
definition: A representation of the Lie algebra [sl(2)](c:sl-2) of traceless $2\times2$ matrices over $\mathbb{C}$ is a complex [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ with [linear maps](c:linear-map) $E,F,H$ on $V$ such that $[H,E]=2E$, $[H,F]=-2F$ and $[E,F]=H$. Every finite-dimensional one is a direct sum of [irreducible](c:irreducible-representation) representations $V_n$ of dimension $n+1$, on which $H$ has the eigenvalues $n,n-2,\dots,-n$.
examples: The standard representation $\mathbb{C}^2$ has $E=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $F=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $H=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$.
The homogeneous polynomials of degree $n$ in two variables form the irreducible representation $V_n$.
Non-example: $E=F=0$ and $H=\mathrm{id}$ on $\mathbb{C}$ is not a representation, because $[E,F]=0$ is not equal to $H$.

steps: Take the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{sl}_2$, with the basis $E$, $F$ and $H$.
A representation of $\mathfrak{g}$ is a Lie algebra homomorphism $\mathfrak{g}\to\mathfrak{gl}(V)$.
The images of the three basis elements $E$, $F$ and $H$ determine such a map.
These images must obey the three bracket relations, and any triple that obeys them gives a representation.
links.why: It shows that an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ representation is a triple of operators with three relations, so it is easy to test.

reminder: The smash product of two pointed spaces is their product with the wedge sum collapsed to a point.
definition: For [pointed spaces](c:pointed-space) $(X,x_0)$ and $(Y,y_0)$, the smash product is $X\wedge Y=(X\times Y)/(X\vee Y)$, where $X\vee Y=X\times\{y_0\}\cup\{x_0\}\times Y$ is the [wedge sum](c:wedge-sum) seen inside the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product). The [quotient space](c:quotient-space) has the collapsed point as base point. For spectra, the smash product is the analogous product with the [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum) as unit.
examples: The smash product of spheres is a sphere: $S^m\wedge S^n\cong S^{m+n}$.
For every pointed space $X$, the smash product $X\wedge S^0$ is $X$.
The smash product $X\wedge S^1$ is the reduced suspension of $X$.
Non-example: the wedge sum $X\vee Y$ is the subspace of $X\times Y$ that the smash product collapses, so it is not the smash product.

steps: Write the circle $S^1$ as the interval $[0,1]$ with its end points identified to the base point.
The smash product $S^1\wedge X$ collapses the sets $\{0,1\}\times X$ and $[0,1]\times\{x_0\}$ to one point.
This quotient of $[0,1]\times X$ is the reduced suspension $\Sigma X$.
So the reduced suspension is the smash product with $S^1$, a special case.
links.why: It shows that suspension is smashing with a circle, so facts about smash products give facts about suspensions.

reminder: A localization $L$ of spectra is smashing when $LX$ is the smash product of $X$ with the localized sphere $LS$.
definition: A [Bousfield localization of spectra](c:bousfield-localization-of-spectra) $L$ is smashing when the natural map $X\wedge LS\to LX$ is an equivalence for every spectrum $X$, where $S$ is the [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum) and $\wedge$ is the [smash product](c:smash-product). Equivalently, $L$ preserves all [coproducts](c:coproduct) of spectra.
examples: The identity localization $LX=X$ is smashing, because $LS=S$ and $X\wedge S=X$.
Rationalization is smashing: $LS=H\mathbb{Q}$ and $LX=X\wedge H\mathbb{Q}$.
Localization at a prime $p$ is smashing: $LX=X\wedge S_{(p)}$, where $S_{(p)}$ is the sphere spectrum with the other primes inverted.
Non-example: $p$-completion is a Bousfield localization that is not smashing, because it does not preserve infinite direct sums.

steps: Take a [Bousfield localization](c:bousfield-localization-of-spectra) $L$ of spectra, with its natural map $X\to LX$ to the local spectrum.
Add the condition that $L$ preserves arbitrary coproducts.
Then $X\wedge LS\to LX$ is an equivalence for every $X$.
So the single spectrum $LS$ determines $L$, and $L$ is smashing.
links.why: It shows that a smashing localization is a Bousfield localization given by smashing with one fixed spectrum.

reminder: A smoothing operator $S_t$ is close to the identity and gains $k$ derivatives of smoothness at the cost of a factor $t^k$.
definition: Let $F$ be a graded [Fréchet space](c:frechet-space) with [seminorms](c:seminorm) $\|\cdot\|_0\le\|\cdot\|_1\le\cdots$, such as $C^\infty$ with norms that measure $n$ derivatives. A family of [linear maps](c:linear-map) $S_t:F\to F$ for $t\ge1$ is a family of smoothing operators when $\|S_tf\|_n\le C\,t^{n-m}\|f\|_m$ for $n\ge m$ and $\|f-S_tf\|_n\le C\,t^{n-m}\|f\|_m$ for $n\le m$, with constants $C$ that depend only on $m$ and $n$. This is the sense used in the Nash-Moser theorem.
examples: On $C^\infty(S^1)$ with the Sobolev norms $\|f\|_n^2=\sum_k(1+k^2)^n|\hat f(k)|^2$, the truncation $S_tf=\sum_{|k|\le t}\hat f(k)e^{ikx}$ of the [Fourier series](c:fourier-series) is a smoothing operator.
Non-example: the family $S_t=\mathrm{id}$ is not smoothing, because $\|f\|_n\le C\|f\|_m$ for $n>m$ fails on the functions $e^{ikx}$ with $k$ large.

reminder: A polynomial is solvable when every root comes from its coefficients by field operations and $n$-th roots.
definition: Let $K$ be a [field](c:field) of characteristic $0$. A [polynomial](c:polynomial) $f\in K[x]$ is solvable by radicals when all its roots in an [algebraic closure](c:algebraic-closure) lie in a field $K(a_1,\dots,a_r)$ with $a_1^{n_1}\in K$ and $a_i^{n_i}\in K(a_1,\dots,a_{i-1})$ for each $i$. By Galois theory, this holds exactly when the [Galois group](c:galois-group) of $f$ is a [solvable group](c:solvable-group).
examples: Every polynomial of degree at most $4$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is solvable, by the quadratic, cubic and quartic formulas.
The polynomial $x^n-a$ is solvable for every $n$, because its roots are $\sqrt[n]{a}$ times roots of unity.
Non-example: $x^5-4x+2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ has Galois group $S_5$, which is not solvable, so its roots have no formula with radicals.

reminder: The radical of a Lie algebra is its largest solvable ideal.
definition: Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a finite-dimensional [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) over a field. Its radical $\mathrm{rad}(\mathfrak{g})$ is the sum of all [solvable](c:solvable-lie-algebra) [Lie ideals](c:lie-ideal) of $\mathfrak{g}$, which is itself a solvable ideal and so the largest one. The quotient $\mathfrak{g}/\mathrm{rad}(\mathfrak{g})$ is [semisimple](c:is-semisimple).
examples: A semisimple Lie algebra such as $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ has radical $0$.
A solvable Lie algebra, such as the algebra of upper triangular matrices, is its own radical.
Over a field of characteristic $0$, the radical of $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ is its center, the scalar matrices.
Non-example: the center is not the radical in general; for the algebra with $[x,y]=y$ the center is $0$, but the radical is the whole algebra.

reminder: The space complexity of an algorithm is the number of memory cells it uses, as a function of the input length.
definition: For a [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) $M$ that halts on every input, the space used on an input $w$ is the number of work-tape cells that $M$ visits. The space complexity of $M$ is the function $s(n)$ that gives the largest space used on inputs of length $n$; for a nondeterministic machine, the maximum runs over all computation branches. The space complexity of a problem is the smallest growth rate among the machines that solve it, and such bounds define [complexity classes](c:complexity-class).
examples: Deciding whether a binary string is a palindrome needs only $O(\log n)$ cells on a machine with a read-only input tape, because it stores two positions.
Deciding whether a Boolean formula is satisfiable needs $O(n)$ cells, because the machine tries each assignment in turn and reuses the same cells.
Non-example: the number of steps of a machine is its time complexity, not its space complexity; a counter that uses $O(n)$ cells can run for $2^n$ steps.

reminder: A finite spectrum has a dual, its function spectrum into the sphere spectrum, with evaluation and coevaluation maps.
definition: Two [finite spectra](c:finite-spectrum) $X$ and $Y$ are Spanier-Whitehead dual when there are maps $Y\wedge X\to S$ and $S\to X\wedge Y$ that satisfy the triangle identities, where $S$ is the [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum) and $\wedge$ is the [smash product](c:smash-product). The dual of $X$ is the [function spectrum](c:function-spectrum) $DX=F(X,S)$, and a spectrum in the [stable homotopy category](c:stable-homotopy-category) has a dual exactly when it is finite.
examples: The sphere $S^n$ has the dual $S^{-n}$, and a finite wedge of spheres has the wedge of the opposite spheres as its dual.
For a finite complex $K$ embedded in $S^{n+1}$, the complement $S^{n+1}\setminus K$ is dual to $K$ up to a shift of $n$, which is Alexander duality in stable form.
Non-example: the Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectrum $H\mathbb{Z}$ is not finite, so it has no Spanier-Whitehead dual.

steps: The [stable homotopy category](c:stable-homotopy-category) is a [symmetric monoidal category](c:symmetric-monoidal-category) with the smash product and the unit $S$.
In such a category, a dual of $X$ is an object $DX$ with an evaluation map and a coevaluation map that obey the triangle identities.
Spanier-Whitehead duality is exactly this data for the smash product.
So it is duality of [dualizable objects](c:dualizable-object) here, and the dualizable spectra are the finite ones.
links.why: It shows that Spanier-Whitehead duality is the general duality of a monoidal category in the stable homotopy category.

reminder: A special cube complex is a nonpositively curved cube complex whose hyperplanes avoid four bad behaviors.
definition: A [nonpositively curved](c:curvature) cube complex $X$ made of [cubes](c:cube) is special when its hyperplanes, the midcubes glued across the cubes, behave well. No hyperplane is one-sided, none crosses itself, none is directly self-osculating, and no two hyperplanes inter-osculate. For a finite complex this holds exactly when there is a local isometry from $X$ to the Salvetti complex of a right-angled Artin group.
examples: Every graph, seen as a one-dimensional cube complex, is special, because each hyperplane is a single point.
The torus $T^n$ with its cube structure is special, as the Salvetti complex of $\mathbb{Z}^n$.
The fundamental group of a closed hyperbolic $3$-manifold has a finite-index subgroup that is the fundamental group of a compact special cube complex (Agol and Wise).
Non-example: a Möbius band made of three or more squares in a row is nonpositively curved but has a one-sided hyperplane, its core curve, so it is not special.

reminder: A sphere bundle is a fibre bundle whose fibre is a sphere.
definition: A sphere bundle is a [fibre bundle](c:fibre-bundle) $\pi:E\to B$ that is locally trivial with fibre the [sphere](c:sphere) $S^n$. For a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $V\to B$ of rank $n+1$ with a metric, the unit sphere bundle $S(V)=\{v\in V:|v|=1\}$ is the main example.
examples: The trivial bundle $B\times S^n\to B$ is a sphere bundle.
The unit tangent bundle of a surface is a sphere bundle with fibre $S^1$.
The Hopf fibration $S^3\to S^2$ is the unit sphere bundle of the tautological line bundle over $\mathbb{CP}^1$, with fibre $S^1$.
Non-example: the disc bundle $D(V)\to B$ has a closed ball as fibre, so it is not a sphere bundle.

steps: Take a fibre bundle $\pi:E\to B$ with fibre $F$ and local trivializations $\pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times F$.
Choose the fibre $F$ to be the sphere $S^n$.
Then every fibre is a sphere, and the transition functions are maps from overlaps into homeomorphisms of $S^n$.
So $E\to B$ is a sphere bundle.
links.why: It shows that sphere bundles inherit all the theory of fibre bundles, with a sphere as the fixed fibre.

reminder: A spherical function is a $K$-invariant joint eigenfunction of the invariant operators on $G/K$ that has value $1$ at the base point.
definition: Let $G$ be a [locally compact group](c:locally-compact-group) and $K$ a [compact](c:compact-group) subgroup such that $(G,K)$ is a Gelfand pair. A spherical function is a continuous function $\varphi:G\to\mathbb{C}$ with $\varphi(e)=1$, with $\varphi(k_1gk_2)=\varphi(g)$ for $k_1,k_2\in K$, and with $\int_K\varphi(xky)\,dk=\varphi(x)\varphi(y)$, where $dk$ is the normalized [Haar measure](c:haar-measure) of $K$. For a semisimple [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$ with maximal compact subgroup $K$, these are the $K$-invariant joint eigenfunctions of the $G$-invariant differential operators on the [homogeneous space](c:homogeneous-space) $G/K$, normalized to $1$ at the base point.
examples: On the sphere $S^2=\mathrm{SO}(3)/\mathrm{SO}(2)$, the spherical functions are the Legendre polynomials $P_k(\cos\theta)$, the zonal spherical harmonics with value $1$ at the pole.
On $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the space of the Euclidean motion group modulo $\mathrm{SO}(n)$, they are the averages of plane waves over all directions, which are Bessel functions.
Non-example: the harmonic $\sin\theta\cos\phi$ on $S^2$ is a Laplace eigenfunction but is not invariant under rotation about the pole, so it is not a spherical function.

steps: Take $G=\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and $K=\mathrm{SO}(2)$, so that $G/K$ is the sphere $S^2$.
A $K$-invariant function on $S^2$ depends only on the polar angle $\theta$, so write it as a function of $x=\cos\theta$.
For such functions, the Laplace eigenvalue equation becomes Legendre's differential equation in $x$.
Regularity on the whole sphere gives eigenvalue $-k(k+1)$, and the solution with value $1$ at $x=1$ is $P_k(x)$.
links.why: It shows that Legendre polynomials are the spherical functions of the pair $(\mathrm{SO}(3),\mathrm{SO}(2))$.

reminder: An object has spherical symmetry when every rotation about a fixed center leaves it unchanged.
definition: A function, set or tensor field on $\mathbb{R}^3$ is spherically symmetric about a point $p$ when it is invariant under all rotations about $p$, that is, under the [special orthogonal group](c:special-orthogonal-group) $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ fixing $p$. A [spacetime](c:spacetime) is spherically symmetric when $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ [acts](c:group-action) on it by [isometries](c:isometry) whose orbits are $2$-spheres.
examples: The Newtonian potential $\phi(x)=-GM/|x|$ depends only on $|x|$, so it is spherically symmetric.
The [Schwarzschild metric](c:schwarzschild-metric) is spherically symmetric: the $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ orbits are the spheres of constant $t$ and $r$.
Non-example: the potential $\cos\theta/|x|^2$ of a point dipole is invariant only under rotations about one axis, so it is axially symmetric but not spherically symmetric.

reminder: A spinᶜ Dirac operator is the Dirac operator on the spinor bundle of a spinᶜ structure, using a connection that includes a $U(1)$ part.
definition: Let $M$ be an oriented [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) with a [spinᶜ structure](c:spinc-structure), with [spinor bundle](c:spinor-bundle) $S$, and let $A$ be a unitary [connection](c:connection) on the determinant line bundle. The Levi-Civita connection and $A$ give a connection $\nabla$ on $S$, and the spinᶜ Dirac operator is $D_A=\sum_ie_i\cdot\nabla_{e_i}$, where $e_i$ is a local orthonormal frame and the dot is Clifford multiplication. It is a first-order elliptic [Dirac operator](c:dirac-operator) on sections of $S$.
examples: On a [spin manifold](c:spin-manifold), the spinᶜ structure with trivial determinant line bundle gives the usual spin Dirac operator.
On a Kähler manifold, the canonical spinᶜ structure has spinor bundle $\Lambda^{0,*}T^*M$, and the operator is $\sqrt2(\bar\partial+\bar\partial^*)$.
Non-example: the Wu manifold $SU(3)/SO(3)$ has $W_3\ne0$, so it has no spinᶜ structure and no spinᶜ Dirac operator.

steps: A Dirac operator is a first-order operator $D=\sum_ic(e_i)\nabla_{e_i}$ on a [Clifford module bundle](c:clifford-module-bundle) with a compatible connection.
The spinor bundle $S$ of a spinᶜ structure is a Clifford module bundle, with Clifford multiplication $c$.
The connection built from the Levi-Civita connection and $A$ is compatible with this multiplication.
So $D_A$ is a Dirac operator on a bundle of spinors twisted by a line bundle.
links.why: It shows that spinᶜ Dirac operators have all the properties of Dirac operators, such as ellipticity and an index.

reminder: A short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ splits when the map $B\to C$ has a section, so that $B\cong A\oplus C$.
definition: In an abelian category, a short [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) $0\to A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{g}C\to0$ is split when $g$ has a [section](c:section) $s:C\to B$ with $gs=\mathrm{id}_C$. Equivalently, $f$ has a left inverse $r:B\to A$ with $rf=\mathrm{id}_A$, so that $A$ is a [retract](c:retract) of $B$; equivalently, there is an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) $B\cong A\oplus C$ that turns $f$ and $g$ into the inclusion and the projection of the [direct sum](c:direct-sum).
examples: The sequence $0\to A\to A\oplus C\to C\to0$ with the inclusion and the projection always splits.
Every short exact sequence of vector spaces splits, because a basis of $C$ lifts to $B$.
Non-example: $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$ does not split, because $\mathbb{Z}$ is not isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$.

steps: Start with a short exact sequence $0\to A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{g}C\to0$.
Add the condition that $g$ has a [section](c:section) $s$ with $gs=\mathrm{id}_C$.
Then $f$ has a left inverse $r$, and the map $(r,g):B\to A\oplus C$ is an isomorphism.
So the sequence is the trivial one for $A\oplus C$, and no twisting remains.
links.why: It shows that splitting is the extra condition that makes an extension trivial.

reminder: A symmetry is spontaneously broken when the action has it but the chosen ground state does not.
definition: Let a group $G$ [act](c:group-action) on a [configuration space](c:configuration-space) so that an [action functional](c:action-functional) $S$ is $G$-invariant. The symmetry is spontaneously broken when a minimum $\phi_0$ of $S$, a vacuum, is not fixed by $G$; its [stabilizer](c:stabilizer) $H$ is then a proper subgroup of $G$, and $G$ moves $\phi_0$ to other minima. In quantum theory, the same idea applies to vacuum states.
examples: The potential $V(\phi)=\lambda(|\phi|^2-v^2)^2$ of a complex field is invariant under $\phi\mapsto e^{i\alpha}\phi$, but every minimum $|\phi|=v$ moves under this rotation, so $U(1)$ is broken.
A ferromagnet below the Curie temperature has rotation-invariant laws, but its magnetization picks one direction.
Non-example: $V(\phi)=\tfrac12m^2\phi^2$ with $m^2>0$ is invariant under $\phi\mapsto-\phi$ and has the single vacuum $\phi=0$, which this symmetry fixes, so nothing is broken.

reminder: A sporadic group is a finite simple group that is not cyclic, not alternating and not of Lie type.
definition: A sporadic finite simple group is a [finite simple group](c:finite-simple-group) that lies in none of the infinite families of the classification. These families are the cyclic groups of prime order, the [alternating groups](c:alternating-group) $A_n$ with $n\ge5$ and the [groups of Lie type](c:group-of-lie-type). There are exactly $26$ sporadic groups, from the [Mathieu group](c:mathieu-group) $M_{11}$ of order $7920$ to the [Monster group](c:monster-group).
examples: The Mathieu group $M_{11}$ of order $7920$ is sporadic; it acts $4$-transitively on $11$ points.
The Monster group has order about $8\times10^{53}$ and is the largest sporadic group.
Non-example: $A_5$ is a finite simple group, but it is an alternating group, so it is not sporadic.

steps: Start with a finite simple group $G$.
List the infinite families: cyclic groups of prime order, alternating groups and groups of Lie type.
Keep only the groups $G$ that lie in none of these families.
These are the sporadic groups, and by the classification there are $26$ of them.
links.why: It shows that the sporadic groups are the finitely many exceptions in the list of finite simple groups.

reminder: A square is a quadrilateral with four equal sides and four right angles.
definition: A square is a [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral) whose four sides have equal length and whose four [angles](c:angle) are all right angles, that is, $90^\circ$. In coordinates, the unit square has the vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(1,1)$ and $(0,1)$.
examples: The unit square with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(1,1)$ and $(0,1)$.
A square with side $s$ has area $s^2$ and diagonals of length $s\sqrt2$.
Non-example: a rhombus with angles $60^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ has four equal sides but no right angle, so it is not a square.

steps: Start with a [rectangle](c:rectangle), a quadrilateral with four right angles.
Add the condition that two adjacent sides have equal length.
Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, so all four sides are then equal.
So the rectangle is a square.
links.why: It shows that a square is a rectangle with equal sides, so every fact about rectangles holds for squares.

reminder: A polynomial is square-free when it has no repeated root in the algebraic closure of its field.
definition: Let $F$ be a [field](c:field) and $\overline F$ its [algebraic closure](c:algebraic-closure). A [polynomial](c:polynomial) $q\ne0$ with coefficients in $\overline F$ is square-free when $(x-a)^2$ does not divide $q$ for any $a\in\overline F$, that is, when $q$ has no repeated root. Equivalently, $q$ and its derivative $q'$ have no common root, so $\gcd(q,q')=1$.
examples: The polynomial $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$ is square-free.
The polynomial $x^2+1$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is square-free, because its roots $\pm i$ are different.
Non-example: $x^3-x^2=x^2(x-1)$ is not square-free, because $x^2$ divides it and $0$ is a double root.

reminder: A square matrix has the same number of rows as columns.
definition: A square matrix of size $n$ over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ is an $n\times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) $A=(a_{ij})$ with entries $a_{ij}\in R$. The square matrices of size $n$ form the [matrix algebra](c:matrix-algebra) $M_n(R)$, in which the product of two of them is again an $n\times n$ matrix.
examples: The [identity matrix](c:identity-matrix) $I_n$ and the zero matrix are square matrices of size $n$.
The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ is a square matrix of size $2$.
Non-example: a $2\times3$ matrix has $2$ rows and $3$ columns, so it is not square.

steps: Take an $n\times m$ [matrix](c:matrix) $A$ with $n$ rows and $m$ columns.
Add the condition $n=m$.
Then $A$ is a square matrix, and you can multiply two such matrices of the same size in either order.
links.why: It shows that square matrices are matrices with the extra property that makes powers and determinants possible.

steps: Start with a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})$.
Add the condition $a_{ij}=0$ whenever $i\ne j$.
Then $A$ is a [diagonal matrix](c:diagonal-matrix), determined by its $n$ diagonal entries.
links.why: It shows that a diagonal matrix is a square matrix whose off-diagonal entries all vanish.

steps: Start with a real square matrix $A$.
Add the condition $A^TA=I$, where $A^T$ is the [transpose](c:transpose-matrix).
Then the columns of $A$ are orthonormal, and $A$ is an [orthogonal matrix](c:orthogonal-matrix).
links.why: It shows that an orthogonal matrix is a real square matrix with the transpose as inverse.

reminder: The stabilizer formalism describes a quantum state by the abelian group of Pauli operators that fix it.
definition: Let $P_n$ be the [Pauli group](c:pauli-group) on $n$ [qubits](c:qbit). A stabilizer group is an abelian subgroup $S\subset P_n$ with $-I\notin S$; if $S$ has $n$ independent generators, it fixes a unique [state](c:quantum-state) up to phase, namely the common $+1$ [eigenvector](c:eigenvector) of all elements of $S$. The formalism stores the generators of $S$ instead of the $2^n$ amplitudes, and it updates them under Clifford gates and Pauli measurements.
examples: The state $|0\cdots0\rangle$ has the stabilizer group generated by $Z_1,\dots,Z_n$.
The Bell state $(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)/\sqrt2$ has the stabilizer group generated by $X\otimes X$ and $Z\otimes Z$.
Non-example: the state $(|0\rangle+e^{i\pi/4}|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ is an eigenvector of no Pauli operator except the identity, so it is not a stabilizer state.

reminder: A stable homotopy group is the colimit of the homotopy groups of ever higher suspensions of a space.
definition: For a pointed space $X$ and an integer $n$, the stable homotopy group is $\pi_n^s(X)=\operatorname{colim}_k\pi_{n+k}(\Sigma^kX)$, where the maps of the [sequential colimit](c:sequential-colimit) send a class to its [suspension](c:suspension). For a connected CW complex $X$, the [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group) in this sequence become isomorphisms once $k$ is large enough, by the Freudenthal suspension theorem. For $X=S^0$ these are the stable stems $\pi_n^s$.
examples: The stable stems start with $\pi_0^s=\mathbb{Z}$ and $\pi_1^s=\mathbb{Z}/2$, generated by the Hopf map $\eta$.
The third stable stem is $\pi_3^s=\mathbb{Z}/24$.
Non-example: $\pi_3(S^2)\cong\mathbb{Z}$ is an unstable group; the stable group $\pi_1^s$ is $\mathbb{Z}/2$, and one reaches it only after suspending.

reminder: A stable map is a holomorphic map from a nodal curve with marked points that has only finitely many automorphisms.
definition: A stable map to a space $X$ is a holomorphic map $f:C\to X$ from a connected [nodal curve](c:nodal-curve) $C$ with $n$ distinct smooth marked points, such that the automorphisms of $C$ that fix the marked points and commute with $f$ form a finite group. Equivalently, every contracted component of genus $0$ has at least $3$ special points (nodes or marked points), and every contracted component of genus $1$ has at least $1$. [Gromov-Witten invariants](c:gromov-witten-invariants) count stable maps; for an [orbifold](c:orbifold) target, the curve may carry orbifold points at the nodes and markings.
examples: The map $\mathbb{P}^1\to\mathbb{P}^1$, $z\mapsto z^d$ with $d\ge1$ and no marked points is stable, because only the $d$-th roots of unity fix it.
Every map from a smooth curve of genus at least $2$ is stable, even a constant map, because such a curve has finitely many automorphisms.
Non-example: the constant map from $\mathbb{P}^1$ with two marked points is not stable, because the automorphisms that fix both points form the infinite group $\mathbb{C}^*$.

reminder: The stable orthogonal group is the union of all the groups $O(n)$ under the inclusions $O(n)\subset O(n+1)$.
definition: Let $O(n)\to O(n+1)$ be the inclusion $A\mapsto\mathrm{diag}(A,1)$ of [orthogonal groups](c:orthogonal-group). The stable orthogonal group is the [sequential colimit](c:sequential-colimit) $O=\operatorname{colim}_nO(n)=\bigcup_nO(n)$ with the colimit topology, so it is a [topological group](c:topological-group). Its elements are the infinite orthogonal matrices that equal the identity outside a finite block.
examples: A matrix of $O$ is $\mathrm{diag}(R_\theta,1,1,\dots)$ for a rotation $R_\theta$ of the plane.
Bott periodicity gives $\pi_k(O)$ for $k=0,\dots,7$ as $\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2,0,\mathbb{Z},0,0,0,\mathbb{Z}$, and then the groups repeat with period $8$.
Non-example: the infinite matrix $\mathrm{diag}(-1,-1,-1,\dots)$ is orthogonal but is not the identity outside a finite block, so it is not in $O$.

reminder: The stable unitary group is the union of all the groups $U(n)$ under the inclusions $U(n)\subset U(n+1)$.
definition: Let $U(n)\to U(n+1)$ be the inclusion $A\mapsto\mathrm{diag}(A,1)$ of [unitary groups](c:unitary-group). The stable unitary group is the [sequential colimit](c:sequential-colimit) $U=\operatorname{colim}_nU(n)=\bigcup_nU(n)$ with the colimit topology, a [topological group](c:topological-group). Its [classifying space](c:classifying-space) is $BU=\operatorname{colim}_nBU(n)$.
examples: Bott periodicity gives $\pi_k(U)=\mathbb{Z}$ for odd $k$ and $\pi_k(U)=0$ for even $k$.
The determinant $\det:U\to U(1)$ exists on all of $U$ and induces an isomorphism $\pi_1(U)\cong\mathbb{Z}$.
Non-example: $U(2)$ is not stable, because $\pi_4(U(2))\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ but $\pi_4(U)=0$.

reminder: A vector bundle is stable when every coherent subsheaf of smaller rank has strictly smaller slope than the bundle.
definition: Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety with a fixed polarization, so that every [coherent sheaf](c:coherent-sheaf) has a [degree](c:degree-of-a-coherent-sheaf). The [slope](c:slope-of-a-coherent-sheaf) of a sheaf $F$ of positive [rank](c:rank-of-a-coherent-sheaf) is $\mu(F)=\deg(F)/\mathrm{rk}(F)$. A [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $E$ is stable when $\mu(F)<\mu(E)$ for every coherent subsheaf $F\subset E$ with $0<\mathrm{rk}\,F<\mathrm{rk}\,E$, and semistable when $\mu(F)\le\mu(E)$.
examples: Every line bundle is stable, because it has no subsheaf of rank strictly between $0$ and $1$.
The tangent bundle of projective space $\mathbb{P}^n$ is stable.
Non-example: $\mathcal{O}\oplus\mathcal{O}$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$ is semistable but not stable, because the subsheaf $\mathcal{O}$ has the same slope $0$.
Non-example: $\mathcal{O}(1)\oplus\mathcal{O}$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$ is unstable, because the subsheaf $\mathcal{O}(1)$ has slope $1$, which is above the slope $1/2$ of the bundle.

steps: Take a holomorphic [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $E$ on $X$, seen as a locally free coherent sheaf.
Compute the slope $\mu(E)$ and the slope of each coherent subsheaf of $E$.
Add the condition that every subsheaf of rank between $0$ and $\mathrm{rk}\,E$ has smaller slope.
Then $E$ is stable, which makes it a well-behaved point of the moduli space of bundles.
links.why: It shows that stability is a numerical condition on subsheaves added to a vector bundle.

reminder: The stack of $G$-local systems on $X$ has the local systems as points and their isomorphisms as arrows.
definition: For a space $X$ and an [algebraic group](c:algebraic-group) $G$, the stack of $G$-local systems $\mathrm{Loc}_G(X)$ is the [moduli stack](c:moduli-stack) of $G$-[local systems](c:local-system) on $X$ and their isomorphisms. It sends a test scheme $S$ to the groupoid of families of $G$-local systems on $X$ parametrized by $S$. When $X$ is connected with a finitely generated [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) $\pi_1(X)$, it is the [quotient stack](c:quotient-stack) $[\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_1(X),G)/G]$ for the conjugation action.
examples: For $X$ a point, $\mathrm{Loc}_G(X)$ is the classifying stack $BG=[\mathrm{pt}/G]$.
For $X=S^1$, $\mathrm{Loc}_G(S^1)$ is $[G/G]$, the quotient of $G$ by conjugation.
Non-example: the character variety $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_1(X),G)/\!/G$ is a coarse moduli space, because it forgets the automorphism groups of local systems that the stack remembers.

reminder: The state space of a system is the set of all states in which the system can be.
definition: The state space of a system is the set, often with extra structure, whose points are the possible states of the system at one moment. For a classical mechanical system it is the [phase space](c:phase-space) of positions and momenta. For an algebra of observables such as a unital [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra) $A$, it is the [convex set](c:convex-set) of states, which are the [positive linear functionals](c:positive-linear-functional) $\omega$ on $A$ with $\omega(1)=1$.
examples: A particle on a line has the state space $\mathbb{R}^2$ of pairs of position and momentum.
A qubit has the state space of density matrices, which is a closed ball, the Bloch ball.
A finite automaton has its finite set of internal states as state space.
Non-example: the set of measurement outcomes is not the state space; for a qubit measured in the $Z$ basis there are two outcomes, but the states form a three-dimensional ball.

steps: A classical Hamiltonian system has a position $q$ and a momentum $p$ for each degree of freedom.
Its state at one time is the point $(q,p)$.
The set of all such points is the [phase space](c:phase-space).
So phase space is the state space of a classical Hamiltonian system.
links.why: It shows that phase space is the classical case of a state space.

reminder: A spacetime is static when it has a timelike Killing vector field that is orthogonal to a family of hypersurfaces.
definition: A [spacetime](c:spacetime) is static when it is [stationary](c:stationary-spacetime), with a timelike [Killing vector field](c:killing-vector-field) $\xi$, and $\xi$ is orthogonal to a family of [hypersurfaces](c:hypersurface), that is, $\xi^\flat\wedge d\xi^\flat=0$. Then the metric has the form $g=-N^2dt^2+h$, where the function $N$ and the Riemannian metric $h$ on the slices do not depend on $t$.
examples: Minkowski spacetime is static, with $\xi=\partial_t$.
The exterior of the [Schwarzschild spacetime](c:schwarzschild-spacetime) is static, with $\xi=\partial_t$.
Non-example: the Kerr spacetime is stationary but not static, because its Killing field $\partial_t$ is not hypersurface orthogonal, as the black hole rotates.

steps: Start with a stationary spacetime that has a timelike Killing vector field $\xi$.
Form the one-form $\xi^\flat=g(\xi,\cdot)$.
Add the condition $\xi^\flat\wedge d\xi^\flat=0$, which says that $\xi$ has no twist.
By the Frobenius theorem, the orthogonal spaces of $\xi$ then form hypersurfaces, and the spacetime is static.
links.why: It shows that static means stationary with no rotation.

reminder: A stochastic process is stationary when its joint distributions do not change under a shift in time.
definition: A [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $(X_t)_{t\in T}$ with $T=\mathbb{Z}$ or $T=\mathbb{R}$ is stationary when, for every shift $s$ and all times $t_1,\dots,t_k$, the [joint distribution](c:joint-distribution) of $(X_{t_1+s},\dots,X_{t_k+s})$ equals that of $(X_{t_1},\dots,X_{t_k})$. In words, the law of each trajectory is unchanged by a rigid time translation.
examples: A sequence of independent random variables with the same law is stationary.
A [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) that starts in its stationary distribution is a stationary process.
The process $X_t=A\cos t+B\sin t$ with independent standard normal $A$ and $B$ is stationary.
Non-example: [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) is not stationary, because $\mathrm{Var}(B_t)=t$ changes with $t$, although its increments are stationary.

steps: Start with a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $(X_t)$ and its joint distributions of finitely many times.
Shift all the time indices by the same amount $s$.
Add the condition that every joint distribution stays the same under every such shift.
Then $(X_t)$ is stationary.
links.why: It shows that stationarity is a time-shift invariance added to a stochastic process.

steps: Let $(X_n)$ be [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) with common law $\mu$.
The joint law of $(X_{n_1},\dots,X_{n_k})$ for distinct indices is the product $\mu^{\otimes k}$.
A shift of the indices keeps them distinct and gives the same product measure.
So an iid sequence is stationary, and stationarity allows dependence between the terms.
links.why: It shows that stationarity extends the iid case to processes with dependence.

reminder: A statistic is a function of the sample whose formula does not depend on the unknown distribution.
definition: Let $X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ be a sample, that is, [random variables](c:random-variable) drawn from a distribution with unknown parameters. A statistic is a [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $T=t(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ of the sample, where the formula $t$ does not involve the unknown parameters. Since $t$ is measurable, $T$ is again a random variable.
examples: The sample mean $\bar X=\frac1n\sum_iX_i$ is a statistic.
The sample maximum $\max_iX_i$ and the sample variance $\frac1{n-1}\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2$ are statistics.
Non-example: $(\bar X-\mu)/\sigma$ for an unknown mean $\mu$ and an unknown standard deviation $\sigma$ is not a statistic, because its formula uses the unknown parameters.

steps: A sample $X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ is a random vector on a probability space.
A statistic is $T=t\circ X$ for a measurable function $t$.
A measurable function of a random vector is a [random variable](c:random-variable).
So every statistic is a random variable, and the extra condition is that $t$ does not depend on unknown parameters.
links.why: It shows that a statistic has a distribution of its own, which is the basis of estimation and testing.

reminder: The Steenrod squares are natural additive operations $\mathrm{Sq}^i$ on mod $2$ cohomology that raise degree by $i$ and commute with suspension.
definition: The Steenrod squares are homomorphisms $\mathrm{Sq}^i:H^n(X;\mathbb{Z}/2)\to H^{n+i}(X;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ of [ordinary cohomology](c:ordinary-cohomology), defined for all spaces $X$ and all $i\ge0$, natural in $X$ and compatible with the [suspension](c:suspension) isomorphisms. They satisfy $\mathrm{Sq}^0=\mathrm{id}$, $\mathrm{Sq}^n(x)=x\cup x$ for $\deg x=n$, $\mathrm{Sq}^i(x)=0$ for $i>\deg x$, and the Cartan formula $\mathrm{Sq}^k(x\cup y)=\sum_{i+j=k}\mathrm{Sq}^i(x)\cup\mathrm{Sq}^j(y)$, which uses the [cup product](c:cup-product).
examples: The square $\mathrm{Sq}^1$ is the [Bockstein homomorphism](c:bockstein-homomorphism) of the sequence $0\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to\mathbb{Z}/4\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$.
In $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^\infty;\mathbb{Z}/2)=\mathbb{Z}/2[x]$ one has $\mathrm{Sq}^i(x^n)=\binom{n}{i}x^{n+i}$.
Non-example: the squaring map $x\mapsto x\cup x$ on $H^2(-;\mathbb{Z})$ is natural but not additive, because $(x+y)^2=x^2+2xy+y^2$, so it is not a Steenrod square.

steps: Take the map $\mathrm{Sq}^i:H^n(X;\mathbb{Z}/2)\to H^{n+i}(X;\mathbb{Z}/2)$.
It exists for every space $X$ and commutes with every map $f$, that is, $f^*\mathrm{Sq}^i=\mathrm{Sq}^if^*$.
So $\mathrm{Sq}^i$ is a natural transformation between two cohomology functors, a [cohomology operation](c:cohomology-operation).
The special case adds that it is additive and commutes with suspension.
links.why: It shows that Steenrod squares are the stable additive cohomology operations in mod $2$ cohomology.

reminder: A step function is constant on each interval of a finite partition of the real line.
definition: A function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a step function when there are finitely many points $a_1<\dots<a_k$ such that $f$ is [constant](c:constant-function) on each of the intervals $(-\infty,a_1)$, $(a_1,a_2)$, $\dots$, $(a_k,\infty)$. The values at the points $a_i$ themselves are arbitrary. Equivalently, $f$ is a finite linear combination of indicator functions of [intervals](c:interval).
examples: The Heaviside function, with $H(x)=0$ for $x<0$ and $H(x)=1$ for $x\ge0$, is a step function.
The indicator function of $[0,1)$ is a step function, and so is every finite sum of such functions with coefficients.
Non-example: the floor function $\lfloor x\rfloor$ is constant on each interval $[n,n+1)$, but it has infinitely many jumps, so it is not a step function.

steps: Let $f$ be a [constant function](c:constant-function) on $\mathbb{R}$.
Choose no jump points, so $k=0$.
Then $\mathbb{R}$ is the one interval on which $f$ is constant.
So every constant function is a step function with no jumps.
links.why: It shows that step functions allow finitely many jumps where constant functions allow none.

steps: Let $f$ be a step function with jump points $a_1<\dots<a_k$.
For any set $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, the preimage $f^{-1}(B)$ is a union of some of the intervals and some of the points $a_i$.
A finite union of intervals and points is a Borel set.
So $f$ is a [measurable function](c:measurable-function), and its integral is a finite sum.
links.why: It shows that step functions are measurable and can approximate other functions in integration theory.

reminder: Stereographic projection maps the sphere minus one point onto Euclidean space along the lines through that point.
definition: Let $S^n=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:|x|=1\}$ be the [sphere](c:sphere) and $N=(0,\dots,0,1)$ its north pole. The stereographic projection $\sigma:S^n\setminus\{N\}\to\mathbb{R}^n$ sends $x$ to the point where the line through $N$ and $x$ meets the plane $x_{n+1}=0$, so that $\sigma(x)=(x_1,\dots,x_n)/(1-x_{n+1})$. It is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) onto [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$, with inverse $\sigma^{-1}(y)=(2y,|y|^2-1)/(|y|^2+1)$.
examples: For $n=1$, the circle minus the north pole maps onto the real line by $(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi)\mapsto\cos\varphi/(1-\sin\varphi)$.
For $n=2$, the projection identifies the sphere minus a point with the plane, and adding the point at infinity gives the [Riemann sphere](c:riemann-sphere).
The projections from the north pole and the south pole form an [atlas](c:atlas) of $S^n$ with the transition map $y\mapsto y/|y|^2$.
Non-example: the orthogonal projection of $S^n$ onto the plane $x_{n+1}=0$ is not injective, because the points $(x',t)$ and $(x',-t)$ have the same image.

steps: The formula for $\sigma$ is continuous on $S^n\setminus\{N\}$, because $1-x_{n+1}\ne0$ there.
The formula for $\sigma^{-1}$ is continuous on all of $\mathbb{R}^n$, because $|y|^2+1\ne0$.
A direct check gives $\sigma\sigma^{-1}=\mathrm{id}$ and $\sigma^{-1}\sigma=\mathrm{id}$.
So $\sigma$ is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) from the punctured sphere onto $\mathbb{R}^n$.
links.why: It shows that the punctured sphere and Euclidean space are the same topological space, by an explicit map.

reminder: The Stiefel-Whitney classes of a real vector bundle are natural mod $2$ cohomology classes that multiply under direct sum.
definition: The Stiefel-Whitney classes of a real [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $E\to X$ are classes $w_i(E)\in H^i(X;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ with $w_0=1$ and total class $w=1+w_1+w_2+\cdots$. They are natural, $w(f^*E)=f^*w(E)$, and vanish in degrees above the rank of $E$. The class of a direct sum $E\oplus F$ is the [cup product](c:cup-product) of $w(E)$ and $w(F)$, and $w_1$ of the tautological line bundle over $\mathbb{RP}^1$ generates $H^1(\mathbb{RP}^1;\mathbb{Z}/2)$.
examples: A trivial bundle has total class $w=1$.
For the tautological line bundle $\gamma$ over $\mathbb{RP}^n$, $w(\gamma)=1+a$, where $a$ generates $H^1(\mathbb{RP}^n;\mathbb{Z}/2)$.
A bundle $E$ is orientable exactly when $w_1(E)=0$, so a manifold $M$ is [orientable](c:orientation-of-a-manifold) exactly when $w_1(TM)=0$.

Non-example: the Chern classes $c_i(E)\in H^{2i}(X;\mathbb{Z})$ of a complex bundle are integral classes, so they are not Stiefel-Whitney classes, although $c_i$ mod $2$ equals $w_{2i}$ of the underlying real bundle.

steps: A [characteristic class](c:characteristic-class) assigns to each bundle $E\to X$ a class $c(E)\in H^*(X)$ with $c(f^*E)=f^*c(E)$.
Take real vector bundles and the coefficient group $\mathbb{Z}/2$.
Put $c=w_i$, which is natural by the first axiom.
So $w_i$ is a characteristic class, and the sum and normalization axioms single out the Stiefel-Whitney classes.
links.why: It shows that Stiefel-Whitney classes are the characteristic classes of real bundles with mod $2$ coefficients.

reminder: A random variable $X$ is stochastically dominated by $Y$ when $\mathbb{P}(X>t)\le\mathbb{P}(Y>t)$ for every real number $t$.
definition:
A real [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$ is stochastically dominated by $Y$, written $X\le_{st}Y$, when $\mathbb{P}(X>t)\le\mathbb{P}(Y>t)$ for every real $t$. Equivalently, $\mathbb{E}f(X)\le\mathbb{E}f(Y)$ for every increasing function $f$ for which both sides exist, and equivalently there is a coupling of $X$ and $Y$ with $X\le Y$ almost surely. For [probability measures](c:probability-measure) $\mu$ and $
u$ on a [partially ordered set](c:partial-order), $\mu\le_{st}
u$ means $\mu(A)\le
u(A)$ for every increasing set $A$.
examples: If $X\le Y$ pointwise on one probability space, then $X\le_{st}Y$.
If $X$ is exponential with rate $2$ and $Y$ is exponential with rate $1$, then $X\le_{st}Y$, because $e^{-2t}\le e^{-t}$ for $t\ge0$.
Non-example: the normal laws $N(0,1)$ and $N(0,4)$ do not dominate each other, because $\mathbb{P}(X>t)$ is smaller for $t>0$ and larger for $t<0$.

reminder: A stochastic integral of an adapted process against Brownian motion is the mean-square limit of sums of integrand times increment.
definition: Let $X$ be a semimartingale, for example a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$ with its [filtration](c:filtration), and let $H=\sum_iH_i\mathbf 1_{(t_i,t_{i+1}]}$ be a simple [predictable process](c:predictable-process), where $H_i$ depends only on information up to time $t_i$. The stochastic integral is $\int_0^tH\,dX=\sum_iH_i(X_{t\wedge t_{i+1}}-X_{t\wedge t_i})$. For a general integrand it is the limit of these integrals along simple processes that approximate it; for $X=B$ and $\mathbb{E}\int_0^tH_s^2\,ds<\infty$ the limit holds in $L^2$, and the integral is a [martingale](c:martingale).
examples: The integral $\int_0^t1\,dB_s$ equals $B_t$.
The integral $\int_0^tB_s\,dB_s$ equals $\frac12(B_t^2-t)$, which differs from $\frac12B_t^2$ by the Itô correction $-t/2$.
Non-example: the Riemann-Stieltjes integral of $B$ against $B$ path by path does not exist, because Brownian paths have infinite variation; the stochastic integral uses an $L^2$ limit instead.

steps: Let $X=B$ be a Brownian motion, which is a continuous martingale and so a semimartingale.
Take an adapted integrand $H$ with $\mathbb{E}\int_0^tH_s^2\,ds<\infty$.
The stochastic integral $\int H\,dB$ is then the [Itô integral](c:ito-integral).
The general case allows any semimartingale as integrator, with jumps and drift.
links.why: It shows that the Itô integral is the Brownian case of the general stochastic integral.

reminder: A stochastic process algebra is a process algebra whose activities carry exponential rates and whose semantics is a Markov chain.
definition: A stochastic process algebra is a formal language for concurrent systems, with operators such as prefix, choice and parallel composition, in which every activity has a rate $r$ and takes an exponentially distributed time. Its operational semantics maps each model to a labelled continuous-time [Markov chain](c:markov-chain), whose states are the derivatives of the model and whose transition rates come from the rates of the activities. The model is thus a compositional description of a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process).
examples: PEPA is a stochastic process algebra: the term $(\alpha,r).P'$ is a component that does activity $\alpha$ at rate $r$ and then behaves as $P'$.
The stochastic $\pi$-calculus is a stochastic process algebra for mobile processes.
Non-example: the process algebra CCS has no rates, because it records which actions can happen but not how fast, so it is not stochastic.

reminder: The Stone-Čech compactification $\beta X$ is the compact Hausdorff space through which every map from $X$ to a compact Hausdorff space factors uniquely.
definition: The Stone-Čech compactification of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space) $\beta X$ with a continuous map $\iota:X\to\beta X$. Every [continuous](c:continuous-function) map $f:X\to K$ into a compact Hausdorff space $K$ equals $\bar f\circ\iota$ for a unique continuous map $\bar f:\beta X\to K$. In categorical terms, $\beta$ is the left [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) of the inclusion of compact Hausdorff spaces into spaces, and for a [Tychonoff space](c:tychonoff-space) $X$ the map $\iota$ is an embedding with dense image.
examples: If $K$ is compact Hausdorff, then $\beta K=K$.
The space $\beta\mathbb{N}$ is the space of [ultrafilters](c:ultrafilter) on $\mathbb{N}$, with each $n$ identified with the principal ultrafilter at $n$.

Non-example: the one-point compactification $\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$ is compact Hausdorff but is not $\beta\mathbb{N}$, because the bounded function $n\mapsto(-1)^n$ has no continuous extension to it.

steps: A [compactification](c:compactification) of $X$ is a compact Hausdorff space $Y$ that contains $X$ as a dense subspace.
For a Tychonoff space $X$, the map $\iota:X\to\beta X$ is a dense embedding.
So $\beta X$ is a compactification of $X$.
It is the largest one, because every other compactification of $X$ is a quotient of $\beta X$.
links.why: It shows that $ eta X$ is the biggest compactification, and every other one is a quotient of it.

reminder: A normed space is strictly convex when the midpoint of two different unit vectors has norm less than $1$.
definition: A [normed space](c:normed-space) $E$ is strictly convex when $\|x+y\|<2$ for all $x\ne y$ with $\|x\|=\|y\|=1$, that is, $\|(x+y)/2\|<1$. Equivalently, every closed ball is strictly [convex](c:convex-set): the open segment between two points of the ball lies in its interior.
examples: Every [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) is strictly convex, by the parallelogram law.
The spaces $\ell^p$ and $L^p$ with $1<p<\infty$ are strictly convex.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the maximum norm is not strictly convex, because $x=(1,0)$ and $y=(1,1)$ have norm $1$ and $\|(x+y)/2\|=\|(1,1/2)\|=1$.

steps: Let $E$ be uniformly convex: for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that unit vectors with $\|x-y\|\ge\varepsilon$ have $\|(x+y)/2\|\le1-\delta$.
Take unit vectors $x\ne y$ and put $\varepsilon=\|x-y\|>0$.
Then $\|(x+y)/2\|\le1-\delta<1$ for the matching $\delta>0$.
So $E$ is strictly convex, and strict convexity drops the uniform $\delta$.
links.why: It shows that uniform convexity is a quantitative form of strict convexity.

reminder: A string over an alphabet is a finite sequence of symbols from that alphabet.
definition: A string over a set $A$, the alphabet, is a finite [list](c:list) $a_1a_2\cdots a_n$ of elements of $A$, where $n\ge0$ is its length. The set $A^*$ of all strings, with concatenation as product and the empty string $\varepsilon$ as unit, is the [free monoid](c:free-monoid) on $A$.
examples: Over the alphabet $\{a,b\}$ the strings are $\varepsilon$, $a$, $b$, $aa$, $ab$, $ba$, $bb$, and so on.
The string $abba$ has length $4$, and concatenating $ab$ and $ba$ gives it.
Non-example: the infinite sequence $aaa\cdots$ is not a string, because a string is finite.

steps: A [list](c:list) over $A$ is a finite sequence $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ of elements of $A$.
Take $A$ to be a fixed alphabet of symbols.
Write the list without commas and brackets, as $a_1\cdots a_n$.
Then the lists over $A$ are the strings over $A$, and concatenation of lists is concatenation of strings.
links.why: It shows that strings are lists over an alphabet, so list operations apply to strings.
